newsitem.title: CHINA: Saab Air urges smaller planes for China.
newsitem.headline: Saab Air urges smaller planes for China.

text.p: Saab Aircraft International Ltd is urging China to develop local air routes, saying passengers on smaller commuter aircraft alone could total 100 million a year within 20 years, company officials said on Wednesday.

Investment in China's aviation sector had focused on high-capacity jets that could be profitable only by servicing large hub airports, said Martin Craigs, president of Saab Aircraft's Asia/Pacific regional office. That meant Chinese airlines flew to smaller cities only once or twice a week, far below the needs of investors in search of business and markets outside of the booming coastal regions, Craigs and other officials said.

"The narrow body and the wide body jets have been very successful in bringing economic growth to the coastal regions of China," said Torbjorn Karlsson, sales director for the Saab Aircraft Asia/Pacific office.
More frequent connections to more cities would be needed to shift that economic growth inland, Karlsson said.
"To do that you also need smaller aircraft," he said.
Beijing would have to order the development of smaller local airports, against the wishes of many regional officials eager for the prestige of a large facility, Craigs said.
"Easily, 100 million people could be flying commuter aircraft in 20 years' time," he said. "But only if policy decisions are made in two to three years."
Chinese aviation officials have said China's airlines flew 55.5 million passengers in 1996 and expect that figure to rise to 100 million by the year 2010.

Although China had virtually no commuter traffic at present, Saab Aircraft, which is wholly owned by Swedish firm Investor AB, would be poised to capture the lion's share of the future small aircraft market, other officials said.
"The market total could be about 300 aircraft," Karlsson said. "That's about 10 for each province or area."
Saab hoped to sell mainly its 58-seater Saab 2000 propeller-driven aircraft, Karlsson said.
China had not bought any Saab 2000 aircraft yet but airline officials had expressed enthusiasm at the $15 million plane's performance compared with larger jets, he said.
"We are quite confident within the next two to three years we will be able to achieve a hard sell," he said.

The company had sold four of its $10 million, 36-seater Saab 340 airplanes to China Eastern in 1992, and eastern provincial carrier Shandong Airlines was now using the planes on local routes, he said.
